tip.title: Eat the vegetables and protein first
tip.why: The same plate, eaten in a different order, lands differently in your blood. In a 2015 crossover pilot at Weill Cornell, Alpana Shukla's group fed people with type 2 diabetes an identical meal of chicken, salad and bread twice, a week apart: carbohydrate first one week, vegetables and protein first the next. Eating the carbohydrate last cut the glucose rise by roughly a third at 30 and 60 minutes and lowered the insulin response as well. A 2019 follow-up in prediabetes found a similar effect. The samples were small and the people were not healthy volunteers, but the mechanism (fibre and protein slow stomach emptying and blunt the carb hit) applies to anyone, and the cost of trying it is zero.
how: At lunch today, finish the salad, vegetables or beans and the protein before you touch the rice, bread or tortilla; same food, different order.
Eating out, ask for the side salad or soup to come first and leave the bread basket until the mains arrive.
If you want proof, notice the 2 PM slump on a carb-first day versus a vegetables-first day; that dip is the glucose curve you just flattened.
tip.ask: What did you eat first at your last meal, and did you feel the afternoon dip that usually follows it?

pick.name: Cisco Systems
pick.theme: The networking incumbent beat on every line and raised its AI revenue target by 20%, and the stock still fell 6% on Friday
pick.what: Cisco is the largest maker of enterprise and data-center networking gear: Ethernet switches, routers, its Silicon One chips and optics, plus a security business built around Splunk and its firewalls, Webex collaboration and observability software. Roughly half of revenue is now recurring. In AI it sells the back-end and front-end switching that connects GPU clusters at hyperscalers and neoclouds, and AI-ready campus and data-center refreshes to enterprises and governments. Its fiscal year ends in late July, so Thursday's report was the first quarter of fiscal 2027.
pick.why: After Thursday's close Cisco reported first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion against an $18.1 billion consensus and its own $18.0 to $18.2 billion guide, with adjusted earnings of $1.40 a share versus $1.33 expected, product orders up 21% and second-quarter guidance of $1.34 to $1.36 a share, well above the roughly $1.23 the Street had. It raised its fiscal 2027 target for hyperscaler AI infrastructure revenue to $9 billion from $7.5 billion. The shares rose about 5% after hours and then fell 6.24% to 95.64 on Friday as investors focused on slower order growth outside the hyperscalers (up 14% versus 25% last quarter) and on Cisco switching to revenue-based rather than order-based AI disclosure. TipRanks shows a Moderate Buy consensus with 11 Buys and 8 Holds out of 19 and a $137.50 average target; S&P Global's panel rates it Buy with a $133 average; JPMorgan and Bank of America kept Buy at $150. The stock trades about 27% below its June 4 record close of $130. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: Order growth outside the hyperscalers is decelerating, the move to revenue-only AI disclosure can be read as hiding lumpiness, and Morgan Stanley's November 5 downgrade to Equal Weight argues the mix is shifting toward lower-margin AI hardware. Most $135 to $150 targets predate Friday's de-rating. A 10-year yield at 5.15% with a December hike priced in weighs on multiples, Nvidia's report Tuesday and the Anthropic IPO could whipsaw the whole AI-hardware complex, and Arista, Nvidia's Spectrum-X and white-box switches all compete for the same racks. btc.summary: Cowen's newest video, posted Saturday afternoon and titled Bitcoin: The Capitulation Spiral, treats the weekend's slide as the late stage of a four-year cycle rather than a surprise: in his reading, bitcoin tends to capitulate into its cycle low in the months after a US midterm election, and he still expects the weakness to run for weeks, with the Fed's December meeting as the likeliest moment for a final flush. He is watching two levels, the 200-week moving average, which he warns may not hold because prior cycle lows undercut it by around 30%, and the realized price, the average cost basis of all coins, which every previous bear market dipped below before bottoming. A low above realized price would, in his view, only buy a few months before another retest, while a deeper flush would reset the on-chain indicators and set up a cleaner 2027. His practical stance is unchanged: keep dollar-cost averaging rather than trying to call the exact bottom.

brief.lede: SpaceX caught Ship 42 out of orbit on Saturday and Musk blamed the lost booster on thin fuel; Figure is hiring $45-an-hour night-shift robot minders; Tesla's Cybercab contract runs $29,990 plus $299 a month; and bitcoin broke $62,000 overnight.

articles.title: SpaceX catches a Starship from orbit, then explains the lost booster
body: Saturday afternoon SpaceX did the thing it had never done: Ship 42, the upper stage launched on Flight 15 a day earlier, came back from orbit and was caught by the arms of the Starbase launch tower at about **1:20 PM Pacific**, after **14 orbits and roughly 22.5 hours** in space. CNBC, UPI and CBS all described it as the first spacecraft to return from orbit and be caught by the tower it left from, and the first recovery of a Starship upper stage of any kind.

The catch was set up carefully. Three of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites released on Friday carried cameras pointed back at the ship so engineers could inspect the heat shield before committing to a return, and SpaceX said beforehand the shield looked ready. No report on tile or flap condition after the catch had appeared by Sunday morning. Elon Musk posted that he hugged the ship on the pad, and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the catch almost magic and a step closer to the Moon.

The booster got its explanation the same day. Musk said Booster 22 aborted its own catch on Friday because of a slight underperformance of its engines that left it low on fuel, and that the fix is better and more consistent Raptor performance, with another change going into the engine production line. He said the loss does not change the schedule for high-volume, fully reusable flights. No date for Flight 16 has been published; trackers point at December or early 2027.

For SPCX holders the catch lands on Monday, since markets were closed; the stock finished Friday at **$139.11** and slipped about 2% after hours before the catch. Two other threads matter for the price. A Friday filing showed Peter Thiel's Founders Fund entities ended September with about 113 million fewer SpaceX Class A shares than in June, roughly a quarter of the stake and about $17 billion at the September 30 price; the filing does not say whether the shares were sold or distributed to the fund's investors, and the pattern looks like a distribution. And Bloomberg reported that one motive for the proposed Tesla merger is index inclusion: S&P Dow Jones declined to loosen its rules for giant IPOs, so folding into Tesla is a back door into the S&P 500, with TD Securities estimating around **$100 billion** of forced index-fund buying.

What it means: a ship that can be caught is a ship that can be inspected and reflown, which is the whole economic premise of Starship. Watch the condition of Ship 42's shield, whether a Raptor fix makes booster catches routine again, and how SPCX trades Monday. One more orbital-compute note: the Office of Space Commerce named Starcloud, Redwire's SpaceMD, Cowboy Space and Portal Space Systems as the first four companies in its mission-authorization pilot, a path meant to grow into licensing for orbital data centers.

articles.title: Figure hires night-shift robot minders; Foundation's war humanoid
body: The clearest humanoid story this weekend is about the humans. Business Insider, re-reported widely on Friday and Saturday, found that Figure is hiring a night-shift coordinator in Santa Clara at **$40 to $45 an hour**, contract to hire, working 10:30 PM to 7 AM including weekends, to run the overnight operator team and make the calls when a robot breaks with only limited engineering support awake. Humanoids Daily counted nine openings on Figure's internal fleet operations team and about 30 jobs overall devoted to keeping the robots running, with morning and swing coordinators at $35 and operators in San Jose at $30. The listings went up around November 5.

That is a useful counterweight to the autonomy pitch: a company valued near $39 billion is building a shift schedule of people whose job is to watch, reset and test humanoids around the clock, and the robots are now running overnight at customer and internal sites rather than demo-floor hours.

A very different humanoid got its first long profile on Friday. The San Francisco Standard wrote about Foundation, a SoMa startup building humanoids for the battlefield and courting the Pentagon. Its Phantom MK-2 is about **6 feet tall and 200 pounds** in an aluminum shell, dustproof and waterproof, and has not yet had a public debut; earlier reporting had it designed to run about six hours, right itself after a fall, carry up to 80 kilograms and handle firearms with articulated wrists. The company holds a Pentagon test contract and, as the Financial Times reported last week, is in talks with Israel's military over up to 1,000 of the earlier MK-1.

Two European announcements round out the week. A Swiss startup literally named Embodied AI unveiled AIR on Saturday, a wheeled humanoid meant to learn factory tasks on the job and work beside people without safety cages; it says it is already testing with global manufacturers and plans CE marking in 2027, with no price or unit count. And Neura Robotics' partnership with the German utility E.ON and its grid subsidiary enviaM, announced November 5, puts robots trained at a Munich airport gym onto live substations for inspection starting in 2027, with the 4NE1 humanoid named as a candidate platform.

What it means: the humanoid business is splitting into companies that sell robots and companies that sell the operations around them, and Figure is quietly staffing the second kind inside the first. Meta's humanoid, Tesla's Optimus and the actuator supply chain were all quiet over the weekend.

articles.title: Cybercab on sale at $29,990 plus a $299 fee Musk calls too high
body: Tesla opened Cybercab orders to a select group of customers late Friday, and the fine print is the news. The order page lists the two-seat, steering-wheel-free car at **$29,990** before taxes with a $1,000 non-refundable deposit and an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. A **$299 a month** Autonomy Subscription is pre-checked and required to operate the car at all, with one month included. Electrek, TechCrunch and Not a Tesla App all read the agreement the same way: the car works only inside Tesla's Robotaxi service areas, commercial use such as ride-hailing or deliveries is barred without Tesla's permission, and resale is restricted.

Musk reacted within a day. On Saturday he wrote on X that the fee is too high and should match what Full Self-Driving plus connectivity costs on other Teslas, roughly $115 a month, and repeated that the Cybercab will go nationwide as regulators approve it. That leaves early buyers paying for a product whose price the CEO says is wrong and whose operating area is a handful of Texas (and, per Electrek, Florida) geofences smaller than the ones Tesla advertises.

The regulatory piece is unresolved. NHTSA's audit query into how Tesla self-certified the Cybercab against federal safety standards, opened in September, is still open; the standards in question cover foot brakes, turn signals and mirrors, and Tesla never sought the exemption that would let it sell a car without them. Electrek reported this month that Tesla asked the agency to keep its sworn answers confidential. NHTSA has proposed a rule on self-cancelling turn signals but nothing yet on steering wheels.

The merger angle feeds back into the stock. Bloomberg's reporting that a SpaceX combination is partly a route into the S&P 500 helped Tesla to its best five-day run since September 2025 through Wednesday, before Friday's 1.8% dip to **$390.22**. Musk is reportedly pushing for an announcement around the December 3 annual meeting, though it could slip into next year.

What it means: Tesla has turned the Cybercab from a video into a contract, and the contract reads like a robotaxi lease with the buyer providing the capital. Watch whether the monthly fee actually drops to Musk's number before December deliveries, and whether NHTSA closes its audit before the first cars reach customers.

articles.title: Bitcoin breaks $62,000 overnight as $2 billion in bets are wiped
body: The weekend did not hold. After sliding through $67,000 and then $64,000 on Saturday, bitcoin printed a low of about **$61,946** on Coinbase at 1:45 AM UTC Sunday, its weakest since mid-July, before bouncing roughly $3,000 to the mid-$65,000s within two hours. By late Sunday morning UTC it was around $64,500, down about 4% on the day, 15% on the week and more than 21% over the month, and the Fear and Greed index read **10**.

The damage was concentrated in leverage. CoinGlass data cited by BeInCrypto and Yahoo Finance put liquidations across crypto near **$2 billion** in 24 hours, about 87% of it long positions and more than 312,000 traders wiped out; bitcoin alone accounted for roughly $750 million. Crypto.news tied the move to seven straight sessions of spot ETF outflows totalling about $1.91 billion through Thursday, plus a 10-year Treasury above 5%, a strong dollar and a December rate hike priced in. Friday's ETF print was another $185 million out, taking November past $2 billion of outflows. Some traders argued the drop was engineered after bitcoin briefly reclaimed its 50-week average; that is sentiment, not evidence.

Strategy, the largest corporate holder, is now clearly under water. Its 850,364 bitcoin carry an average cost of $75,456, which at the weekend's prices means a paper loss somewhere between $7 billion and $9 billion depending on the hour. Michael Saylor's response on X was to point at his preferred stock: over the past month bitcoin fell 17.3%, he wrote, while the STRC preferred was essentially flat and its dividends left holders slightly positive. The company's next weekly purchase filing is due Monday, and its removal from MSCI indexes takes effect after the close on November 30.

In Washington the center of gravity has moved to the CFTC: Chair Michael Selig told CNBC on Thursday that crypto firms are signing up for the agency's new registration regimes rather than waiting for a market-structure bill that is parked until January, and two SEC nominees face the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday.

What it means: the on-chain crowd is watching whether this low holds above the average cost basis of all coins, the level the last two bear markets undercut before bottoming. Monday brings the first ETF flows and the first Strategy filing after the break, and both will be read as a vote on whether the big holders are still buying.

articles.title: Nvidia's first post-Huang earnings, Anthropic's pricing, AI debt
body: The AI week ahead is unusually dense. Nvidia reports its fiscal third quarter on Tuesday after the close, around 1:20 PM Pacific with the call at 2 PM, its first report since Jensen Huang's abrupt exit. Consensus compiled by LSEG and others sits near **$109 billion** of revenue and about $2.48 of adjusted earnings per share, against $96.2 billion last quarter, and options were pricing a move of roughly 9% either way. The succession story kept moving: after the Financial Times reported the board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas, Arm's US-listed shares fell more than 5% and Nvidia about 2%, and the board told Reuters it has not chosen a search firm or engaged any candidate. A social-media report of a memo saying executives threatened to quit could not be verified.

Anthropic prices on Wednesday evening and is expected to start trading Thursday as ANT. The new detail from this weekend's coverage: beyond the 825 million Class A shares offered at $70 to $78, seven strategic investors including Google and Nvidia have agreed to buy about **$26 billion** of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price, and the company carries roughly $111 billion of convertible debt that outlets either include or exclude when they quote a valuation, which is why the headline number ranges from about $916 billion to $1.4 trillion. With the book reported more than six times covered, TradingKey raised the question on Friday of whether it prices above the range.

The money behind all of this is increasingly borrowed. Meta completed about $25 billion of debt financing between November 5 and 12, Goldman counted five AI-related bond deals worth $67 billion since late October and $296 billion of hyperscaler issuance this year, and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday forecast AI capital spending of **$1.66 trillion** next year, up about 75%. Lower down the stack it is getting expensive: CoreWeave's 2031 bonds yielded about 15.5% on Monday after touching 16.7%, Nebius fell 17% in a day on a plan to spend $40 to $45 billion in 2027, and Nscale has raised $5.5 billion of debt against a $44.6 billion Anthropic contract it still has to finance.

What it means: by Thursday night the market will have a post-Huang Nvidia print, a priced Anthropic and the Fed's October minutes, which together decide whether the AI trade's funding costs keep rising. One policy note from Friday: Bloomberg reported the White House AI task force wants agencies to ease cyber-liability rules so AI companies will report serious incidents rather than hide them.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta 805 million euros; DRAM price-fixing suit survives
body: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta **805 million euros**, about $887 million, on Friday over a Facebook feature on Android that has been reading users' photo galleries since 2023. The Garante found the gallery-suggestion feature accessed photos, videos and metadata from roughly 20 million Italian Android users without specific consent or adequate information, and counted a 2019 sanction as an aggravating factor. Meta has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who previously agreed, and to ask for separate consent; it called the fine disproportionate and will appeal. The regulator did not examine whether the images fed AI training, which Meta denies. The fine is under half a percent of Meta's annual revenue.

In California a federal judge declined to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of coordinating to tighten DRAM supply. At the pleading stage the court found that long-term high-bandwidth-memory commitments, Micron's shutdown of its Crucial consumer brand, delayed fabs, the exit from DDR4 and near-identical customer vetting practices plausibly suggest an agreement. Nothing has been proven, but the case now moves to discovery at the exact moment memory prices are the most sensitive input in the PC and phone business.

The supply picture behind that lawsuit shifted this week. Samsung is reported to be putting about $34 billion into HBM packaging capacity roughly 18 months from operating, SK Hynix's chief executive said the shortage could last beyond 2030, and Nvidia is reported to have asked all three memory makers to build HBM base dies on TSMC's 3-nanometer process, which Korean press read as turning them into subcontractors. Against that, China's CXMT is said to be building ten new memory fabs, the kind of capacity that eventually tanks prices.

What it means: Europe's privacy regulators are now landing nine-figure fines on features rather than data breaches, and the DRAM case means the memory makers' pricing power will be argued in court as well as in earnings calls. Both are slow stories that just got a date stamp.

articles.title: A quiet weekend in aging science: a new senolytic lead
body: Nothing new landed in aging research on Saturday or Sunday, so this is a catch-up on unreported items from the past week, with dates. Fight Aging flagged a paper identifying cepharanthine, a plant alkaloid long used in Japan as an anti-inflammatory, as a new senolytic: in the authors' hands it cleared senescent cells, lowered the inflammatory signals those cells secrete and extended lifespan in several model organisms. Species and effect sizes were not available this weekend, so treat it as a lead rather than a result. The same site's Thursday post reviewed the animal evidence for stem cell and exosome therapies and found both show a rejuvenative effect on organ systems, while remaining far from standardized clinical products.

A perspective in the journal Aging, publicized Tuesday, argued that late-life rejuvenation should aim at body-wide signaling networks, the hormones and circulating factors that coordinate tissues, rather than at cellular damage one cell type at a time. A Monday report on an Aging Cell study mapped inflammation-related aging across the heart and found it uneven, with hotspots that could eventually tell cardiologists where to look first.

On the business side, Longeveron said Thursday it has asked the FDA for a meeting after its Phase 2b cell-therapy trial and has begun reviewing all strategic options while conserving cash, which is the language of a company short of runway.

What it means: the field's week was about frameworks and candidates, not results. Watch whether the cepharanthine paper holds up in mice with real survival curves, and whether the signaling-network argument changes what the next trials measure.

vocab.def: A manuscript page that was scraped clean and written over, with traces of the old text still showing; by extension, anything that carries visible layers of its earlier versions.

cards.b: Greek palin ('again') + psēstos ('scraped'): parchment was expensive, so monks scraped off old texts and reused the skin
layered record, overwritten text, accretion; near relatives: patina, sediment, legacy code
a city block with 1920s brick behind a glass facade, a codebase where every refactor left fossils, a face that shows every earlier age

examples: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.
Downtown is a palimpsest of booms, with the cannery brick, the dot-com stucco and the new glass all on one block.
vocab.ex: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.

vocab.def: Relating to or living on the banks of a river or stream; the strip of land, plants and animals that depend on a waterway.

cards.b: Latin ripa ('riverbank'), the same root as the Spanish ribera and the French rive
riverside, streamside, bankside, littoral (for a lake or sea)
the willows along Stevens Creek, a wildlife corridor, the law of who owns a riverbank

examples: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.
Water rights here are riparian: if your land touches the stream, you get a share of it.
vocab.ex: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.

vocab.def: Glowing or flickering softly over a surface; of wit or light, playing lightly and brilliantly without heat.

cards.b: Latin lambere ('to lick'): a flame that licks across a surface without burning it
glowing, flickering, luminous, softly radiant
late sun on the bay, a gas flame on a stove, a friend's light and quick humor

examples: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.
Her lambent wit kept the review going for two hours without anyone noticing the time.
vocab.ex: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.

vocab.def: Casually unconcerned; carefree in a way that shows a light, almost careless lack of worry.

cards.b: French insouciant, from in- ('not') and soucier ('to care'), from Latin sollicitare ('to disturb')
nonchalant, carefree, breezy, unbothered
a surfer shrugging at a wipeout, a founder joking through a bad quarter, a cat on a warm car hood

examples: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.
There's an insouciant charm to a city that closes its best street for a Sunday market.
vocab.ex: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.

vocab.def: The tendency to see meaningful patterns or connections in random or unrelated data.

cards.b: Coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958, from Greek apo- ('away from') and phainein ('to show')
patternicity, false pattern, seeing faces in clouds
a backtest that only looks predictive, a 'trend' in three data points, a conspiracy theory

examples: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.
Robot logs invite apophenia: every glitch looks like a pattern until you count.
vocab.ex: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.

vocab.def: Calm self-confidence, especially in a tense or difficult situation.

cards.b: French 'à plomb', 'according to the plumb line', meaning upright and steady
poise, composure, assurance
handling pressure gracefully: a demo gone wrong, a hard question, a surprise

examples: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.
The robot demo failed, but he recovered with aplomb.
vocab.ex: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.

vocab.def: Impossible to avoid or escape; certain to happen no matter what you do.

cards.b: Latin 'ineluctabilis', from in- (not) + eluctari (to struggle out of)
inescapable, unavoidable, inevitable
fate, deadlines, or facts that no amount of effort changes

examples: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.
He felt the ineluctable pull of the old neighborhood.
vocab.ex: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.

spanish.meaning: It just clicked / now I get it
spanish.note: Literally 'the twenty just dropped on me'. Old Mexican payphones took a 20-centavo coin, and the call connected only when the coin dropped. So 'me cayó el veinte' is the moment the line goes live in your head: you finally understand something that had been sitting in front of you. Everyday, friendly, safe with anyone.

cards.en: Has it clicked for you yet?

cards.es: Hasta ahora me cae el veinte
cards.en: Only now is it sinking in
Oh, I get it now (shorter version)

parts.en: to click, to finally get it

dialog.es: Llevo una hora con este problema y no sale.
dialog.en: I've been on this problem for an hour and it won't work.

dialog.es: ¿Ya revisaste el signo? Acuérdate que va al revés.
dialog.en: Did you check the sign? Remember it goes the other way.

dialog.en: Ah! Now it clicks, that's why it came out negative.

dialog.en: See, sometimes all it takes is a little coffee.

spanish.use: Say it the moment a concept finally makes sense today, especially when it was hiding in plain sight; it tells the other person you were listening.

spanish.meaning: What a drag / I really can't be bothered
spanish.note: Hueva is literally fish roe, but in Mexico it means laziness or boredom. '¡Qué hueva!' is the groan you let out when something tedious lands on you: a rainy Sunday errand, a long meeting, a form. Among friends only; it is mildly crude, so skip it with your boss or your partner's parents.

cards.en: I can't be bothered / it bores me

dialog.es: ¿Vamos al súper? Ya no hay nada en el refri.

dialog.es: Pues ni modo, o vamos o cenamos cereal.
dialog.en: Well, no choice: we go or we have cereal for dinner.

dialog.en: Fine, I'll shake it off and let's go.

spanish.use: Say it, with a groan, when a boring task shows up on a day you wanted off; swap in 'qué flojera' when you are not sure how casual the room is.

spanish.note: Cañón is literally 'cannon' or 'canyon', but in Mexico 'está cañón' means something is hard, heavy or impressive: a tough exam, a brutal commute, a wild story. Tone decides whether it's a complaint or admiration.

cards.en: Same idea, cruder; only with close friends

parts.en: a cannon shot; a hit song

dialog.es: ¿Cómo te fue en la entrevista?
dialog.en: How did the interview go?

dialog.en: And did you pass?

dialog.en: I think so, but they wore me out.

spanish.note: Literally 'what a bear', but in Mexico it's the everyday way to say 'how embarrassing' or 'how awkward', about yourself or someone else. 'Hacer el oso' is to embarrass yourself in public.

parts.en: to make a fool of yourself

dialog.en: Oh well, tomorrow nobody will remember.

spanish.note: Literally 'to little', but in Mexico it's the everyday way to say 'really?' or 'you're kidding' when something surprises you. Flip it to '¿a poco no?' and it means 'right?' or 'isn't it?'

cards.en: No way! / Don't make it up!

dare.title: Order lunch entirely in Spanish
dare.why: You have a gap in the middle of the day before the rain gets going (it should hold off until mid-afternoon). Go to Los Altos Taqueria on Old Middlefield Way, open all day Sunday, stand at the counter and do the whole thing in Spanish: greeting, order, a question about what is good today, pay, thank them. The one rule: if they answer in English, you stay in Spanish anyway, and the phone stays in your pocket.
dare.worth: A phrase you have only read is a fact; a phrase you have said to a stranger who understood you is yours. Memory researchers call it the generation effect: what you produce yourself sticks far better than what you consume, and a slightly nervous counter order is about as live as practice gets.
dare.src: Slamecka and Graf · the generation effect, 1978
